newsitem.title: PERU: Ready or not, Peru hostages glad to be free.
newsitem.headline: Ready or not, Peru hostages glad to be free.

text.p: Some were taken by surprise, some were prepared, but the hostages freed from the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima said on Wednesday they were relieved their 18-week ordeal was over.

Crack Peruvian troops stormed the residence on Tuesday to rescue 72 hostages in an assault that saw two soldiers, one hostage and all 14 Marxist guerrillas killed. The attack was launched as most of the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) gunmen were on the ground floor playing soccer.

"They had organised a football championship and they had three or four teams that played constantly," freed Bolivian Ambassador Jorge Gumucio told local CPN radio. "They were all playing and there were only three guards upstairs. So it was a key moment to launch an attack."
Most of the rebels were killed in the first wave when an explosion blew a hole in the floor where they were playing and troops swarmed in through tunnels and the front door.
President Alberto Fujimori said later that based on the information he had from inside the residence, "I did not doubt for one single second in giving the order for this operation."

Gumucio and several other hostages said they had known about the attack a few minutes in advance. Others were completely in the dark. One was so wrapped up in a gripping game of chess that he realised an attack was taking place only when the first explosions shook the building.

"We were so absorbed in ending the game, so into it, that we only realised what was going on when it was obvious that they were coming in," Luis Chang Ching, a member of the ruling party, told local Panamericana television.

His chess opponent, Jesuit Priest Juan Julio Wicht, who turned down a chance to be freed with 225 other hostages in December, told the network he dismissed an advance warning of the attack as a joke intended to ease the tension.
"I was sitting there and they came up to me and said 'They're going to free us in a few minutes. Stay calm,'" he said. "So I thought it was a joke, because we made lots of black jokes."

All the hostages were on the top floor of the residence, a decision taken by MRTA leader Nestor Cerpa several weeks ago because he feared security forces planned to rescue them through tunnels being dug beneath the property.
Their rescuers then swarmed into building and killed the surviving rebels. "They had some grenades which they threw at the rebels on the second floor and exchanged gunfire," Gumucio said.
Despite the risky assault the former hostages broadly agreed with Fujimori's conclusion that it had been the only way to end Latin America's longest hostage standoff.

"We were facing a psychopath and I think it would have been very difficult for Cerpa to accept reaching a balanced agreement," freed congressman Carlos Blanco Oropeza told the Radioprogramas radio station.
"It was the only way because unfortunately I'm convinced that the peaceful negotiations would never have ended," Gumucio said.
While grateful for their freedom, the hostages had some sympathy for their dead former captors, many just teenagers, with whom they had spent 126 days inside the residence.
"I feel a lot for the youngsters, who were humble people from the Peruvian jungle," Gumucio said. "But we knew from the start that it was either us or them."
